```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                     fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120)
library(censoredGP)
library(ggplot2)
run_stan <- identical(Sys.getenv("CENSOREDGP_RUN_STAN"), "true")
report <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "hiv-paper-analysis.rds",
                            package = "censoredGP"))
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
```

This example revisits the HIV-1 RNA analysis in section 5 of
[Hoffmann et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.70277). It estimates a
population trajectory and patient trajectories while accounting for measurements
below the assay limit. Covariance hyperparameters and the population intercept
are sampled jointly with censored measurements, using proper, explicit priors.

The figures and diagnostics bundled with the package were produced by the
four-chain Stan fit shown below. Ordinary vignette builds use those saved
results, so reading or installing the package does not run MCMC. To rerun the
complete analysis, install CmdStan >= 2.37 and set
`Sys.setenv(CENSOREDGP_RUN_STAN = "true")` before rebuilding this vignette.
The repository's `tools/run-paper-example.R` regenerates the bundled results.

## Describe what was observed

```{r data}
hiv <- hiv_a5055()
head(hiv)
table(hiv$censoring)
length(unique(hiv$subject))
range(hiv$day)
```

There are 365 measurements from 44 patients, collected on days 0 through 205.
Of these, 110 indicate an RNA concentration below 50 copies/mL. We model the
log10 concentration. For a censored row, `log_rna` contains `log10(50)`, the
upper detection limit. It does **not** contain a substituted response used as an
exact measurement. The original RNA column is retained for inspection.

```{r response}
cens(hiv$log_rna[1:8], hiv$censoring[1:8])
```

The interface describes censoring separately at every observation. For example,
the following response combines all four observation mechanisms:

```{r mixed-censoring}
mixed <- data.frame(
  time = c(0, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 1.4),
  value = c(2.8, 1.7, 3.2, 2.0, 1.3),
  type = c("none", "left", "right", "interval", "left"),
  upper = c(NA, NA, NA, 2.4, NA)
)
cens(mixed$value, mixed$type, mixed$upper)
# Fit with: cgp(cens(value, type, upper) ~ time, mixed, priors = ...)
```

For an exact row, `value` is the measured response. It is the upper limit for
left censoring, the lower limit for right censoring, and the lower endpoint for
interval censoring; `upper` supplies the interval's other endpoint. Notice that
the two left-censored rows have different limits. A logical censoring vector is
shorthand for left censored (`TRUE`) versus exact (`FALSE`).

Censoring concerns the noisy **measurement**, not a hard bound on the latent
smooth function. Missing measurements should be omitted rather than coded as
censored. The observation process is assumed to be described by the supplied
value bounds; informative missingness and time-to-event survival models require
additional modeling.

## Model and priors in scientific units

For patient $g$, the model is

\[
y_g(t) = \beta_0 + \mu(t) + \eta_g(t) + \epsilon_g(t),
\qquad \epsilon_g(t) \sim N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

Both $\mu$ and the patient deviations use squared exponential kernels,
$k(s,t) = a^2\exp\{-(s-t)^2/(2\ell^2)\}$, with separate amplitudes and length
scales. Patient deviations have marginal variance $k_\eta(t,t)$ and cross-patient
covariance $-k_\eta(s,t)/(44-1)$, enforcing $\sum_g\eta_g(t)=0$. Thus the
population curve is $\beta_0+\mu(t)$ and each patient curve adds its deviation.

We extend the manuscript's zero prior mean by estimating a constant intercept
$\beta_0$ with a proper prior. Set `mean = 0` to use the manuscript's zero-mean
specification; that removes the intercept parameter and its prior. We also
replace the original example's empirical Bayes hyperparameter estimates with
joint Bayesian inference.

```{r priors}
priors <- cgp_priors(
  intercept = normal_prior(3, 1.5),
  amplitude = student_t_prior(4, 0, 2),
  lengthscale = lognormal_prior(log(60), 0.7),
  group_amplitude = normal_prior(0, 1),
  group_lengthscale = lognormal_prior(log(35), 0.7),
  sigma = normal_prior(0, 0.5)
)
knitr::kable(prior_summary(priors))
```

Amplitude and noise parameters are standard deviations in log10 copies/mL;
length scales are in days. Positive parameters with normal or Student-t priors
use the corresponding distribution restricted to values above zero. The
intercept's normal prior is unrestricted.

The intercept prior is centered on 1,000 copies/mL and is broad on the log10
scale: its central 95% interval is approximately 0 to 6 log10 copies/mL. The
population length-scale prior has median 60 days and a central 90% interval of
about 19 to 190 days. The corresponding patient length-scale prior has median
35 days and an interval of about 11 to 111 days. These encode smooth changes
over weeks to months while allowing shorter changes. The half-normal noise
prior places 95% of its mass below approximately 0.98 log10 units. Population
and patient amplitudes permit substantial variation.

These are substantive starting priors in the assay and follow-up units, rather
than priors fitted to the observed responses. They are not universally suitable
for another assay or time scale. The typed constructors validate their arguments,
and changing any prior does not recompile Stan. The other available families are
`gamma_prior()`, `inv_gamma_prior()`, and `exponential_prior()`.

Check the implied prior curves before fitting:

```{r prior-check, eval=run_stan}
grid <- data.frame(day = seq(min(hiv$day), max(hiv$day), length.out = 80))
prior <- prior_predictive(log_rna ~ day, transform(grid, log_rna = 0),
                          priors = priors, ndraws = 200, seed = 56)
```

```{r prior-plot, echo=FALSE}
if (!run_stan) {
  grid <- report$grid
  prior <- report$prior
}
draw_table <- function(draws, locations, n = 20) {
  selected <- seq_len(min(n, nrow(draws)))
  data.frame(day = rep(locations$day, each = length(selected)),
             draw = rep(selected, times = nrow(locations)),
             value = as.vector(draws[selected, , drop = FALSE]))
}
ggplot(draw_table(prior$latent, grid), aes(day, value, group = draw)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.45, color = "#176487") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(50), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "log10 RNA (copies/mL)",
       title = "Prior population curves", subtitle = "20 draws; dashed line: assay limit")
```

This plot concerns the common population component. It intentionally includes
very broad trajectories; a prior predictive check is an opportunity to reject
implausible assumptions before inspecting the fit. To check complete patient
curves and noisy measurements, pass a grouped design to `prior_predictive()` and
inspect its `latent` and `response` matrices. Responses in that design are ignored.

## Fit the full Bayesian model

```{r fit, eval=run_stan}
fit <- cgp(cens(log_rna, censoring) ~ day | subject, hiv,
  priors = priors, kernel = "exp_quad", mean = "constant",
  group_structure = "sum_to_zero", parameterization = "quantile",
  chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4,
  iter_warmup = 1000, iter_sampling = 1000,
  adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12, seed = 1627,
  sig_figs = 18
)
summary(fit)
diagnostics(fit)
```

The population and patient function values are integrated out analytically.
Only censored noisy measurements are augmented, together with covariance
parameters and the intercept. The quantile parameterization is an exact
triangular change of variables with its Jacobian included. Its likelihood and
derivatives are implemented in C++ and used by Stan NUTS. It avoids numerical
integration of a multivariate normal rectangle probability. A directly bounded
augmentation is available through `parameterization = "bounded"` and targets
the same posterior.

There is no low-rank kernel approximation, independence approximation, or
empirical Bayes plug-in estimate. Monte Carlo summaries still have sampling
error. Dense factorization costs O(n³) time and O(n²) memory, so runtime grows
with the number of observations.

```{r diagnostics-table, echo=FALSE}
fit_summary <- if (run_stan) summary(fit) else report$summary
parameters <- as.data.frame(fit_summary$parameters)
knitr::kable(parameters[, c("variable", "mean", "sd", "q5", "q95",
                           "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")], digits = 3)
sampler <- fit_summary$diagnostics
knitr::kable(data.frame(chain = seq_along(sampler$num_divergent),
  divergences = sampler$num_divergent,
  tree_depth_hits = sampler$num_max_treedepth, BFMI = sampler$bfmi), digits = 3)
```

The reported run has `r sum(sampler$num_divergent)` divergent transitions and
`r sum(sampler$num_max_treedepth)` maximum-tree-depth hits. The largest
hyperparameter R-hat is `r sprintf("%.4f", max(parameters$rhat))`; the smallest
bulk effective sample size is `r round(min(parameters$ess_bulk))`.
These checks support using this run for the summaries below. They do not replace
checking prior sensitivity or model adequacy. Sampling took
`r round(fit_summary$elapsed)` seconds on the development machine, excluding
compilation and prediction; this is a record of one run, not a general benchmark.

```{r censored-diagnostics, echo=FALSE}
censored_diagnostics <- if (run_stan) {
  posterior::summarise_draws(posterior::as_draws(fit, variables = "y_cens"))
} else report$censored_diagnostics
```

The 110 augmented censored measurements were checked too: their largest R-hat
is `r sprintf("%.4f", max(censored_diagnostics$rhat))` and smallest bulk
effective sample size is `r round(min(censored_diagnostics$ess_bulk))`.

## Population and patient curves

Draws from `posterior_epred()` include latent function uncertainty as well as
hyperparameter and censored-measurement uncertainty. Each row is a joint curve;
dependence across locations is retained. The method's name denotes draws of the
conditional expected measurement, which is the latent smooth function here.

```{r population-prediction, eval=run_stan}
population_draws <- posterior_epred(fit, grid, component = "population",
                                    ndraws = 800, seed = 53)
```

```{r curve-helper, include=FALSE}
curve_summary <- function(draws, locations) {
  interval <- apply(draws, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
  cbind(locations, mean = colMeans(draws), lower = interval[1, ], upper = interval[2, ])
}
if (!run_stan) population_draws <- report$population_draws
population <- curve_summary(population_draws, grid)
```

```{r population-plot, echo=FALSE}
ggplot(population, aes(day, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "#2878A0", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(color = "#176487", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = hiv, aes(y = log_rna, shape = censoring), alpha = 0.25) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(none = 16, left = 25), name = "Observation",
                     breaks = c("none", "left"), labels = c("Exact", "Left censored")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(50), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "log10 RNA (copies/mL)",
       title = "Population trajectory", subtitle = "Pointwise 95% credible interval") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

As in the manuscript's illustration, inspect patients 1, 9, and 41:

```{r individual-prediction, eval=run_stan}
individual_grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("1", "9", "41"), function(subject) {
  transform(grid, subject = factor(subject, levels = levels(hiv$subject)))
}))
individual_draws <- posterior_epred(fit, individual_grid, ndraws = 800, seed = 54)
# The package also offers: plot(fit, type = "latent", groups = c("1", "9", "41"))
```

```{r individual-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4}
if (!run_stan) {
  individual_grid <- report$individual_grid
  individual_draws <- report$individual_draws
}
individual <- curve_summary(individual_draws, individual_grid)
patients <- hiv[as.character(hiv$subject) %in% c("1", "9", "41"), ]
ggplot(individual, aes(day, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "#2878A0", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(color = "#176487", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = patients, aes(y = log_rna, shape = censoring), size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(none = 16, left = 25), name = "Observation",
                     breaks = c("none", "left"), labels = c("Exact", "Left censored")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(50), linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(vars(subject), nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "log10 RNA (copies/mL)",
       title = "Patient trajectories", subtitle = "Pointwise 95% credible intervals") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Triangles show upper limits, rather than exact measurements at those limits.
The intervals describe smooth functions; an individual latent function can be
above an assay limit even when a noisy measurement is censored below it.
These are pointwise intervals, not simultaneous bands over the whole curve.
For inference on a trajectory's minimum, integral, or differences across times,
calculate that quantity on each joint draw from `posterior_epred()`.

For quick pointwise summaries, `predict(fit, newdata, type = "population")`
avoids constructing a full prediction covariance. For new patients, fit
`group_structure = "independent"`; the sum-to-zero specification is defined
over the original cohort and cannot be extended to unseen groups unchanged.

## Posterior predictive checks and imputation

`posterior_predict()` draws future noisy measurements at the requested
locations, preserving their joint dependence. To reproduce this assay's
censoring event, apply the 50-copy threshold to these draws:

```{r predictive-check, eval=run_stan}
replicated <- posterior_predict(fit, ndraws = 400, seed = 55)
replicated_fraction <- rowMeans(replicated < log10(50))
observed_fraction <- mean(hiv$censoring == "left")
```

```{r predictive-plot, echo=FALSE}
if (!run_stan) {
  replicated_fraction <- report$predictive_censoring_fraction
  observed_fraction <- report$observed_censoring_fraction
}
ggplot(data.frame(fraction = replicated_fraction), aes(fraction)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#2878A0", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_fraction, color = "#B54832", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Fraction below 50 copies/mL", y = "Posterior predictive replicates",
       title = "Does the model reproduce the amount of censoring?",
       subtitle = "Vertical line: observed fraction")
```

The observed fraction is `r sprintf("%.3f", observed_fraction)`; the central
90% posterior predictive interval is
`r paste(sprintf("%.3f", quantile(replicated_fraction, c(0.05, 0.95))), collapse = " to ")`.
This checks one feature of the data. Further checks should examine changes over
time, between-patient variation, residual patterns, and sensitivity to priors
and kernel choice.

Imputing the original censored measurements is a different operation. Each
imputed measurement must satisfy the bounds that were actually observed:

```{r imputation, eval=run_stan}
imputed <- impute_censored(fit)
left <- hiv$censoring == "left"
stopifnot(all(imputed[, left, drop = FALSE] <= log10(50)))
stopifnot(all(imputed[, !left, drop = FALSE] ==
                rep(hiv$log_rna[!left], each = nrow(imputed))))
```

These assertions were checked on every retained draw when generating the
bundled analysis. For mixed censoring, `impute_censored()` returns columns in
the original data order and respects each row's lower and upper limits.

## Keep the fitted model and inspect its implementation

```{r save-fit, eval=FALSE}
saveRDS(fit, "hiv-fit.rds")
fit <- readRDS("hiv-fit.rds")
posterior::as_draws(fit)  # draws with iteration and chain dimensions
prior_summary(fit)      # indicates which priors are active
cgp_stancode()          # the complete Stan program
```

The saved model contains the posterior draws and model information needed for
prediction. It does not require the original Stan CSV output. Compiled models
are cached separately in a user-writable directory.

The bundled run used CmdStan `r report$provenance$cmdstan`, package version
`r report$provenance$package`, seed `r report$provenance$seed`, and four chains
with 1,000 warmup and 1,000 retained iterations each. Its source hash and
generation time are recorded in `hiv-paper-analysis.rds` alongside the actual
posterior curve draws and diagnostics.
